instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ.

documents.original:
Families bringing toddlers often leave before the credits. Reserve blanket space beside the exit path so those departures do not set off a chain of people standing up. Pool loungers sit much higher than picnic rugs. Mark a chair area behind the blankets while there is still daylight and late arrivals will know where they can unfold a seat. The grass between the gate and the picnic tables gets soft after watering. Set aside viewing places along the paved strip so wheelchair users can sit with their friends. The snack counter normally takes cash from members. Print prices and payment methods on the invitation so a family can bring the right change or pack its own picnic.

Several nearby homes face the lawn across a narrow lane. Aim the speakers into the audience and listen from the lane during the sound check to catch dialogue that carries into bedrooms. Even on a quiet evening, wind can swallow a softly spoken line. Turn on captions and have somebody read them from the back row before admitting guests. Light from the changing rooms helps people find the toilets but washes out the picture when the door swings open. A freestanding shade beside the doorway can protect the image while leaving the route bright. For someone arriving alone, a full lawn can look like a collection of private parties. Have a greeter keep track of gaps and offer to show newcomers an open spot.

A small child looking for a parent may remember the striped snack awning more easily than a volunteer's name. Introduce it as the meeting place during the welcome. A forecast that changes during the afternoon can send families on a wasted trip. Give the groundskeeper a decision time and publish the rain update where people found the original invitation. A streaming subscription may cover only household viewing. Secure permission for the outdoor screening before announcing the title so the club can advertise a film it can actually show. The club secretary has to return borrowed gear the next morning. Keep its packing boxes together with the lenders' names so teardown volunteers can put the right remote and cables back with each machine.
documents.rewrite:
Before the club puts a film title on a flyer, get the right to show it on the lawn. The person with the streaming account may only have permission to play it at home. Include the snack prices and ways to pay on the flyer too. A family unfamiliar with the counter's usual cash sales to members can then turn up with change or bring supper along. Agree on an afternoon deadline for the groundskeeper to make the weather call, and post the decision wherever the invitation ran so people see it before they set out.

Walk the grounds while they're still light. Mark where chairs can go behind the picnic rugs, since even an ordinary pool lounger will block the view from a blanket and people arriving in the dark will need to know where to put it. Leave some blanket spots along the way out for families whose toddlers won't last the whole film. They can slip away without getting a row of neighbors to their feet. Save room to watch together on the paved stretch for wheelchair users and their companions. The lawn on the way from the gate to the tables can be quite soft after it's been watered. Ask someone at the entrance to keep an eye on the spaces that are left. An offer to walk over to one can make all the difference to a lone arrival facing a lawn of established groups.

At rehearsal, point the speakers toward the crowd and send someone across to the narrow lane to hear whether people in the houses opposite will be getting the dialogue in their bedrooms. Put the captions on as well and check that someone at the very back can read them before the gates open. A breeze can take away a quiet line even with little other noise. Try opening the changing-room door with the film playing. A portable screen beside the door can intercept the light falling on the picture and still let people see their way to the toilets. During the welcome, point out the striped awning at the snack stand as the place to meet if separated. A little child is more likely to recall the stripes than a helper's name. Save the equipment cartons in one place with the lenders identified. Whoever packs up can match cables and remotes to their machines, ready for the secretary's return trip in the morning.

documents.original:
People may bring a sewing machine expecting a sewing volunteer to repair the motor. Describe a few jobs the volunteers can actually tackle in the invitation so residents can judge whether to make the trip. Carrying a broken lamp across town is work in itself. Remind people to bring its shade, fittings and any loose pieces so a missing part does not prevent a repair. An item may behave perfectly until it is handled a particular way. Ask the owner to describe when the fault appears before anyone takes it apart, preserving clues the bench inspection might miss. Threading a needle is difficult under the hall's high ceiling lights. Put a movable task lamp on the sewing table so the volunteer and the garment's owner can see the stitch clearly.

The hall's folding tables wobble when somebody leans on a vise. Assign clamping jobs to the solid workbench so the neighboring repairer can work without tools creeping toward the edge. A visitor holding a heavy toaster should not have to queue on their feet. Take their name at the door and give them a seat within earshot of the person calling jobs. When a volunteer does every stitch, the same loose button will bring its owner back. Let the visitor finish the last few stitches with guidance so they leave knowing how to repeat the mend. Battery compartments sometimes arrive with obvious leaks. Ask the intake volunteer to flag those items before they reach the shared work surface so the session lead can arrange appropriate handling.

An iron with an intermittent fault can seem fixed the instant the cord is moved. Have the qualified volunteer record the final checks before the item is cleared for collection. If an owner goes home for a missing attachment, another volunteer may inherit the repair. Tie a short work note to the handle so the next person can pick up at the right point. Someone picking up a repaired umbrella will open it as soon as they leave. Clear a patch of floor near collection so the owner can try it with the volunteer still there. Fifteen minutes before the hall closes, opening another clock creates a tableful of parts with nowhere to go. Switch intake to advice and future bookings while the current jobs are wrapped up.
documents.rewrite:
Give examples of what the repairers actually know how to do when you invite the neighborhood. Someone with a dead sewing-machine motor could easily misunderstand what it means to have a sewing volunteer on hand. People who decide it's worth the trip should bring the whole thing, including such bits as a lamp's shade, its fittings and anything that's fallen off. It's a shame to carry a lamp all that way only to find the piece you need is at home.

Have someone at the door take names so a visitor can put down a heavy toaster and sit where they'll hear their turn called. Get the owner's account of exactly what makes the trouble appear before the repairer opens the item. A fault that shows up only with certain handling may leave no clue once it's on the bench. At intake, look for visible battery leaks and flag them for the person leading the morning, who can arrange how to handle them before they go anywhere near the common worktop.

Use the sturdy bench for a vise or anything else that has to be clamped. Leaning on one of the hall's folding tables could shake the next repairer's tools right to the edge. At the sewing station give the pair a lamp they can move close enough to thread the needle and see each stitch under those high overhead lights. Hand the needle over for the last few stitches and talk the visitor through them. They'll know what to do the next time the button comes loose. If somebody steps out to fetch an attachment, fasten a brief account of the work so far to the handle in case a different helper takes over.

Movement of a cord can make a troublesome iron seem to work again. Before releasing it, the volunteer qualified to check it should write down the results of the final checks. Leave room at pickup for an owner to put the repair to use with the helper on hand, even if that means opening an umbrella indoors. For the last quarter hour, offer people advice or a place at a later session and let the benches finish what they've got. Otherwise the next clock you agree to open may still be in pieces at closing time.

documents.original:
Afternoon sun heats the catalog under the front window. Move it to the cooler interior wall so the contents are less likely to deteriorate while waiting for planting season. Gardeners call the same bean by several local names. Put those names on the drawer card beside the variety name so neighbors can recognize the seed they came looking for. A donated jar can contain enough lettuce seed for dozens of gardens. Portion it into small envelopes at a packing afternoon so the first visitor can take a useful amount without emptying the supply. Gardeners may know when they picked a tomato without remembering when they saved the seed. Ask for the harvest year at donation and mark uncertain dates clearly so borrowers can judge older stock.

One community gardener has noticed which beds stay frosty well into spring. Invite her to annotate the sowing calendar with local observations so the printed dates make sense on nearby streets. Seeds sold for ornamental use sometimes come with a coating the library cannot identify. Ask donors for the original label and have staff check it before accepting commercial leftovers. Seeds saved from a supermarket squash may grow quite differently from the parent. Give uncertain parentage a plain-language note so growers who need predictable results can choose another packet. New gardeners sometimes pull up a seedling with the weeds. Ask local growers for pictures of the first leaves and display them beside the cabinet to help visitors recognize what emerges.

A whole drawer of free seed may tempt a visitor to take more than they can plant. Print the approximate number of pots or row length on the label so they can choose enough for their space. The peas that disappear first might simply be the easiest packet to see. Compare the tally with drawer positions before asking donors to devote more of their gardens to that variety. Some neighbors would happily save seed but pick every pod for dinner. Put a reminder out before harvest explaining which plants to leave standing so donors still have mature seed to bring in. An interesting growing note can get lost when a packet changes hands. Keep a notebook near the drawers where borrowers can record how that variety fared on a windy balcony or in heavy soil.
documents.rewrite:
Give the catalog a spot against an inside wall. Seed waiting for its planting season will keep better there than in the heat of the afternoon sun by the front window. Hold a packing afternoon with the gardeners. One person's jar of lettuce seed might supply dozens of households if you divide it into envelopes that give the first person a worthwhile share and leave plenty for others. Say how many pots an envelope should fill, or roughly how much row it will sow. Faced with a drawerful of free packets, people can use that information to take what they have space for.

At the point of donation, ask what year the crop was harvested. Someone who can't place the day they saved the tomato seeds may well remember the harvest. Label doubtful dates as such so people can make their own call on older seeds. Get the original labels for leftover commercial seed and let the staff examine them before accepting it, particularly if ornamental seed has an unfamiliar coating. If the parentage is unclear, explain in everyday words that, for example, seed from a grocery-store squash could produce a very different squash. Someone counting on a particular crop can pick a different envelope. Write the names local growers use for each bean on the drawer card along with its variety so people can find an old favorite.

Put the gardeners' local knowledge where people choosing a packet can see it. The woman who knows which community beds still get frost late in spring could add her observations to the sowing calendar and help neighbors interpret its dates for their street. Photographs from local growers of the first leaves would make a good display by the drawers for beginners who might otherwise weed out their crop. Leave a notebook there too. A borrower can leave word about a variety that did well in heavy soil or on a blustery balcony even after the envelope has gone to somebody else.

Before asking a donor to give up more garden space to the first peas that ran out, check the counts against where each packet sat in the cabinet. The peas might simply have been easiest to spot. And get a reminder to potential donors before they pick their last pods for dinner. Tell them which plants to leave in the garden long enough to provide mature seed for the next round.

documents.original:
The assembly hall has a raised threshold that is barely noticeable on foot. Push a loaded trolley along the delivery route before opening day to find where a ramp or another entrance is needed. The cooking school needs numbers before its pots go on. Have the office send attendance changes at an agreed morning cutoff so the cooks can adjust portions while there is still time. Different classes in the two schools use the same room number. Put the receiving school's name on every carrier so the driver can sort the load correctly at the first stop. Several children receive individualized meals that look much like the standard dish. Have the designated adult match each covered portion with the child's meal record before bringing it to their place.

The hall has one handwashing station near the stage. Let each class wash at its usual sinks on the way down so the lunch queue can keep moving once children arrive. On wet days coats make narrow aisles even tighter. Keep the usual classroom pegs in use for lunch so children carrying trays have a clear path between tables. A child juggling a cup and a tray may spill both on the turn into the hall. Put water jugs on the tables so pupils can sit down before pouring a drink. Some children normally eat in a quieter corner of the dining room. Set a table away from the trolley and loudspeaker so they can keep that part of their lunchtime routine.

The hall's varnished floor makes spilled gravy difficult to see. Station cleaning supplies with the duty adult so a spill can be guarded and wiped before the next group crosses it. A warm carrier gives little indication of the temperature of its contents. Have the trained receiving lead check and log the food under the school's handling procedure before it is served. The hall is needed for afternoon music, and stacked tables can block the instrument cupboard. Mark parking places for furniture with the music teacher so the room is ready for the next lesson. The final delivery crates will still belong to the lending school when the kitchen reopens. Count them against the delivery log during the last collection so staff know what has gone home.
documents.rewrite:
Try the journey from delivery door to lunch tables with a full trolley before the first day. A lip in the assembly hall doorway is easy to step over without noticing it, but the trolley trial will tell you whether to fit a ramp or come in another way. Arrange a time each morning for the office to pass attendance changes to the school making the lunches, early enough for the cooks to change quantities before they start cooking. Ask them to label every carrier with the destination school's name. Both schools have classes with the same room number, and the driver needs to sort things out at the first stop.

On arrival the person trained to receive the delivery should check and record the food temperature as the school's food-handling procedure directs, before anything is served. A carrier can feel warm without telling you much about the meal inside. Assign an adult to check each covered individual meal against the record for the child who needs it and then take it to that child's place. To the eye it may be almost identical to everybody else's lunch.

Get children ready in their classrooms. They can leave coats on their regular pegs, especially in wet weather when coats in the hall would pinch the aisles people need to carry trays. Each class can wash at its familiar sinks on the way to lunch and walk straight in, saving a queue at the single station by the stage. Keep the drinks in jugs on the tables so nobody has to round the corner balancing both cup and tray. Put a table well away from the delivery trolley and the loudspeaker for pupils used to having a quiet place to eat. Keep the cleaning things with the adult on duty. Gravy can be hard to spot against the varnished floor, and the adult can stand guard and clean it up before another class walks through.

Work out with the music teacher where the tables and other furniture should go after lunch and mark the spots. Then the afternoon class can get straight to the instruments without moving a stack of tables away from the cupboard. When the six weeks are up and the kitchen opens again, check off the lending school's crates against the delivery record at the final pickup so everyone knows which ones made it back.

documents.original:
The Moon gives a beginner something recognizable to find with the naked eye. Choose a night when a crescent or quarter Moon will stand above the local roofline during the gathering. Clouds often leave people wondering whether to set off from home. Give the invitation a specific time and place for the go-ahead message, with a reserve evening listed alongside it. A sign that points across a lawn is little help to someone pushing a wheelchair or a buggy. Trace the firm route from the entrance and describe its distance, surface and tightest turn in the invitation. New arrivals naturally look for the busiest spot and can blunder into a tripod. Put the greeting point on the approach path and have someone show them where the telescope legs begin.

Finding a constellation becomes easier when the paper turns with the viewer. Mark one conspicuous landmark on a simple chart so people can line up the page from their actual starting position. A telescope pointed at nothing in particular makes a poor first demonstration. Have its lender align the finder before dusk so the volunteer can return quickly to a target after an accidental bump. People differ in where a sharply focused image appears. Demonstrate the focus knob while the first visitor is at the eyepiece so everyone in earshot knows which control they may adjust. A family waiting behind one observer can feel pressured to take a single hurried glance. Hand out return slips at the telescope so people can explore the sky nearby until their turn comes around.

An invitation to notice one detail gives quiet visitors a way into the conversation. Leave pencils and small cards for people to sketch the boundary between the Moon's lit and shaded portions. Standing on grass feels colder than walking there, especially for an observer waiting a turn. Mention warm layers in the invitation and place a few seats on the sheltered edge of the observing area. Sound carries beyond the common after dusk. Gather small groups close to their guide so directions can be given in a conversational voice that also leaves other observers free to listen. An evening judged by telescope turns alone could overlook the person who finally recognized a constellation. At departure, invite visitors to name one thing they could now find again and use those replies to shape a second gathering.
documents.rewrite:
Work out when a crescent or quarter Moon will be high enough to clear the buildings around the common while people are there. It's a first target even a complete beginner can recognize just by looking up. Alongside the date, give a fallback evening and tell people exactly when and where they can check whether the clouds have put the first one off. Walk the firm way in from the entrance with a wheelchair user or a parent pushing a buggy in mind. A sign pointing over the grass doesn't tell them what that approach is like. Put its length, the ground underfoot and its tightest turn in the invitation. Mention extra layers too. Waiting still on the grass gets much colder than walking across it, so leave a few chairs in a sheltered spot at the edge.

Ask each lender to line up the finder on their telescope before the daylight goes. That way the volunteer can start by showing people an object and find it again quickly if somebody nudges the instrument. Meet people on the path as they come in and point out where the tripod legs are before anyone heads straight for the crowd. As the first guest looks through the eyepiece, show how to use the focus knob and explain within hearing of the others that they can turn it for their own eyes. Give out slips at the telescope for people to come back at their turn. Families can spend the wait looking around nearby and needn't feel the queue behind them allows only a quick peek.

For the part of the evening spent looking up unaided, mark a familiar feature of the common on a simple star chart. Standing at the starting spot, visitors can turn the sheet to match their view and pick out a constellation. A guide can bring a few people close at a time and talk at ordinary volume. Voices travel well past the common after dark and other observers will want to hear their own guides. Set out cards and pencils and suggest drawing where the bright part of the Moon meets the dark. Looking closely at that one detail can give someone who has been quiet something to say. When people go home, ask what they'd be able to find again. Their answers will tell you what to plan for next time, including successes like spotting a constellation that counting turns at the telescopes would miss.

documents.original:
A whole district is difficult to hold in mind on a short walk. Build the route around how the neighborhood uses the river and let each stop reveal a different answer in a resident's voice. The river can be busy enough to drown out the best line in an interview. Test listening positions at the time visitors are likely to walk and move a stop inland if its speech disappears. A visitor following an interview may walk right past the building it describes. Open each stop with one precise visual cue and ask listeners to settle there before the story begins. A row of nearly identical warehouses invites wrong turns. Photograph the distinctive end wall from the direction of travel and reuse that viewpoint on the map where the turn occurs.

A resident's memory lands differently when listeners can inspect something it mentions. Ask interviewees to bring the interviewer to a surviving detail, then record what they notice while standing beside it. An interview may include a family story its speaker later wants to keep private. Play the edited extract to the speaker and agree on its wording, credit and public use before including it. Spoken directions can sound obvious at a desk and fail within seconds on the street. Give an early cut to a newcomer, walk a few paces behind and note where they have to look back. A long street name can be hard to recognize when heard only once. Pair stop titles with the same plain place names on the map, player and direction signs that a visitor will consult.

A visitor who needs a rest should be able to judge how far remains. Mark verified benches and the distance to the next stop on the map, including stretches with nowhere to sit. When a path closes temporarily, a printed arrow can send people to a locked gate. Keep a dated route notice on the tour page with an alternate approach to the affected stop. Not everyone wants to install an app for a half-hour walk. Give the tour a short, readable web address on the starting notice so someone can type it or share it aloud. A listener who knows the area may spot a mistaken name months after launch. Put a correction contact beside each transcript and ask for the stop title so volunteers can locate the disputed passage.
documents.rewrite:
Give the walk one question people can carry with them through the district. How do people here use the river? Pick stops where different residents can each give a different answer. Ask each speaker to take you to a detail that's still there and record what catches their attention as they stand by it. A listener can then look at the very thing that brings the memory back. Give the speaker a chance to hear the edited passage, especially if it touches on family matters they might want to keep to themselves. Settle the wording, the credit and whether you can use it publicly with them before it goes in.

Go out at the hour you expect most people to take the walk and listen from the proposed stopping places. If river traffic swallows a resident's words, try a spot a little farther inland. At the beginning of a track, tell people exactly what feature to look for and ask them to stop there before the interview gets going, or they may get absorbed in the story and pass the building. Where all the warehouses look alike, take a picture of the distinctive end wall as a walker will approach it and put that view at the turn on the map. Use the same straightforward place name for a stop on the player, the map and the signs so visitors can recognize a long street name they only heard once.

Try the first cut on someone new to the neighborhood. Trail them by a few paces and mark where they turn back to you for help. Instructions that seemed perfectly clear while editing can fall apart outside. Check which benches are actually there and put them and the distance to the next stop on the map. A walker deciding when to rest especially needs to see a stretch with no seats ahead. Give the starting sign a web address short and clear enough to type or tell a companion. Few people want a new app just to take a half-hour walk.

Keep the tour page current with a dated notice when part of the route closes. Give another way to reach that stop so nobody follows the printed arrows all the way to a shut gate. Beside each transcript, tell listeners how to contact the volunteers about a correction and ask them to include the stop title. A local resident could recognize a wrong name months later, and that title will take you straight to the passage they heard.

documents.original:
A shelf built from everyone's spare scores may still overlook the players who turn up most often. Ask local groups about their instruments and rehearsal needs, then use their answers to guide the first collection. Two arrangements with the same song title can be completely different to play. Give each entry its arranger, edition and opening tempo marking so borrowers can recognize the version their group rehearses. A clarinet player may search by the instrument in hand and another player by the key heard in the room. Record the part's transposition separately from the work's concert key so both searches make sense. An unfamiliar local composition may find an audience once players hear its shape. When its creator agrees, pair the catalog entry with a short performance excerpt and credit those who made the recording.

Small type on a high shelf is hard to inspect in a busy corridor. Keep a printed browsing binder at seated height and use shelf codes that match the stickers on the music folders. Loose parts can migrate between near-identical folders after rehearsal. Give each part the same collection code as its folder in a removable sleeve, with the instrument name visible at the top. A quartet loses a rehearsal when the second violin part is missing. Put a parts inventory inside the folder and have the borrower and return volunteer check it at opposite ends of the loan. Singling out the only borrower of a rare part on a public sign-out sheet can feel intrusive. Keep contact details in the center's private loan record and show only availability in the browsing catalog.

An entire group may plan around a score being available on a certain evening. Let a named representative reserve the folder for a rehearsal and display the date it is expected back. Penciled bowings from one group can confuse the next one. Supply removable annotation slips and invite ensembles to save their own agreed markings separately when they return a shared set. Many published bindings resist a music stand and can be damaged by forcing them flat. Provide a stand for trying a score at the center so borrowers can see how the edition sits before taking it away. A damaged folder may still look available to someone planning a rehearsal. Mark it awaiting repair in the catalog and describe what needs attention so a volunteer can return it to circulation deliberately.
documents.rewrite:
Start by finding out who'll actually play the music. Ask the local ensembles which instruments they're scoring for and what they'd like to rehearse, and build the first shelves around the answers. A cupboard full of everybody's surplus could still leave the regular players short. Make the catalog specific enough that someone can identify the arrangement their ensemble is learning. The arranger, edition and tempo indication at the beginning distinguish settings of the very same song. Give the transposition of the individual part its own field alongside the concert key of the piece, so the player holding a clarinet and someone looking up a sounding key can both find it. For music by a less familiar local composer, hearing a little of the piece may persuade a group to try it. With the composer's agreement, add a brief clip to the entry and credit the people behind the recording.

Give visitors somewhere to browse at a seated height, using a printed binder with shelf references that match the folder stickers. Nobody should have to decipher tiny titles high up in a crowded corridor. Have a music stand available to try the score in the center before borrowing. Some editions won't sit open comfortably and pressing the binding flat may damage it. Inside each folder, put every part in a removable sleeve marked with the folder's collection code and the instrument clearly visible at the top. That makes it easier to get the music back into the right one of several similar folders. Include a list of parts for the borrower to tick off on the way out and the volunteer to check on return. A quartet can't use its rehearsal time as planned if the second violin part is gone.

Let an ensemble name someone to book a folder for rehearsal, and put the expected return date where other groups planning their evenings can see it. Keep the contact information in a private center record. The public catalog only needs to show availability, particularly when the borrower of an unusual part would be easy to single out. Provide slips that come off for bowings and other rehearsal notes. When the set goes back, encourage the players to retain their group's agreed markings separately so the next players won't be confused by them. If a folder needs mending, update its entry to show it is waiting for repair and say what needs doing. A volunteer can then deal with it and release it for use, and nobody schedules a rehearsal on the assumption it's on the shelf ready to play.

documents.original:
People arriving specifically to contribute may leave boxes in a corridor when the hall is closed. Advertise a staffed intake window and explain where to bring a puzzle during that time. A familiar brand can reuse a box design across several piece counts. Label each donated puzzle with its title and stated count from the manufacturer's panel so people can compare likely commitments. A thousand-piece puzzle with distinct illustrated characters feels different from a thousand pieces of sky. Let contributors add a plain description of the image and the stretches that made their build challenging. People vary in how much a missing piece bothers them. Keep playable incomplete puzzles together and show the known gap on the box image with a removable note so takers can decide.

Boxes come open when they are tilted out of a tight stack. Ask intake volunteers to put loose pieces into a resealable bag and close it before placing the box on the shelf. People with limited grip may find small, thickly packed pieces awkward to handle. Mark large-piece sets by their actual piece size and keep a sample outline on their cards for comparison. A small child may reach whatever is on the bottom shelf while a caregiver browses. Reserve that space for boxed children's puzzles and keep the original age guidance visible on each one. An image printed on the lid may be the only reference available while assembling. Check that the picture is legible and include a clean image from the donor when a damaged lid needs a substitute.

Damp cardboard can spoil the boxes beside it once a cupboard closes. Examine incoming boxes in good light and ask the donor to take back any that show moisture or mildew. People may forget a puzzle's title by the time they discover a problem at home. Give accepted boxes a short identifier so a resident can report an issue without trying to describe the artwork. When a reported missing piece turns up under the dining table, a whole puzzle can become complete again. Keep found pieces in labeled envelopes behind the desk and match them using the puzzle identifier. Neighbors sometimes need to picture a completed puzzle before they choose it. Invite builders to contribute a snapshot for a noticeboard and put its box identifier underneath so someone can look for the same one.
documents.rewrite:
Tell donors which hours someone will be there to receive puzzles and exactly where in the hall to go. Otherwise someone who's made the trip only to find the doors shut may leave a stack of boxes in the passage. Look at each box in good light while its owner is there. Ask them to take a damp or mildewed one home, since it could spoil the cardboard around it inside the closed cupboard. Have the volunteer gather loose pieces in a resealable bag and seal it before shelving the box. A box can tip open as someone pulls it from a tight pile. Check that the picture on the lid is clear enough to build from. It may be the builder's only guide, so if the lid is damaged ask the donor for a clean picture to put with it.

Read the maker's panel for the title and piece count and put both on the exchange label. Boxes from a single brand can look much the same while promising very different amounts of work. Ask the person who's done it to describe the scene in ordinary words and mention any taxing sections. Knowing whether those thousand pieces form individual cartoon figures or endless blue sky tells the next person something a count can't. For the large-piece puzzles, give the actual size of a piece and draw a sample outline on the card. People who have trouble gripping small pieces packed close together can see what they'll be handling. Put boxed children's sets at the bottom with their original age recommendations in plain view, since that's where a little one may reach while the adult is looking.

It's worth shelving still-playable sets with missing pieces together. Use a removable slip on the box picture to show exactly where a known gap is and let the next builder judge whether it matters. Give every box you accept a short code. People who find a problem at home can quote it even if they've forgotten the title and can't describe the scene. A piece first thought lost might simply be under a table. Keep recovered pieces in marked envelopes behind the desk and use the code to get each one back into its puzzle. The same reference works for a display of completed builds. Invite neighbors to pin up a photo with the box code below it, so someone who chooses more easily by seeing the finished puzzle can go and find that set.
